title: Axylus, the host by the roadside
greek: πάντας γὰρ φιλέεσκεν ὁδῷ ἔπι οἰκία ναίων (pantas gar phileesken hodōi epi oikia naiōn)
short: Axylus 'loved' (entertained) every traveller from his house by the road, yet none of those he had welcomed was there to save him.
body: Phileesken here means 'used to treat as a friend', that is, 'used to entertain' (Leaf, Monro): the verb philein in Homer often describes the practical kindness of hospitality (xenia) rather than a feeling. Axylus is 'rich in substance' and 'beloved of all men'; the irony is that none of his guests stands in front of him now to ward off death. The vignette is typical of how the Iliad gives even one-line victims a glimpse of the life they lose. The scene also prepares, by contrast, for the meeting of Glaucus and Diomedes later in the book, where an inherited bond of xenia actually does stop two warriors from killing each other (6.212-31).

title: Supplication and ransom: Adrastus begs for life
greek: λαβὼν ἐλίσσετο γούνων (labōn elisseto gounōn); ζώγρει... δέξαι ἄποινα (zōgrei... dexai apoina)
short: Thrown from his chariot, Adrastus clasps Menelaus' knees, the gesture of a suppliant, and offers ransom (apoina) for his life.
body: Grasping the knees is the ritual gesture of supplication (hiketeia), which placed the suppliant under the protection of Zeus. Adrastus' words, zōgrei, 'take me alive', and the offer of apoina, 'ransom', are the regular formulas (compare 11.130-5, where Agamemnon kills two suppliant sons of Antimachus). Earlier in the war prisoners were often ransomed or sold: Akhilleus had released captives for ransom (11.104-6; 6.425-7, Andromache's mother) and sold Lycaon overseas (21.34-41). Leaf notes that the list of treasure, 'bronze and gold and iron wrought with toil', repeats 11.132-5; iron is valuable here because it was hard to work. The scene is answered at the poem's end, where Priam clasps Akhilleus' knees and the ransom is accepted (24.477-579).

title: Agamemnon's 'just' counsel: kill even the unborn
greek: αἴσιμα παρειπών (aisima pareipōn)
short: Agamemnon demands that no Trojan survive, not even a boy in the womb, and the narrator says he 'counselled aright' (aisima); scholars disagree about this rare authorial judgement.
body: Agamemnon scorns his brother as 'soft' (pepon) and wishes every Trojan to perish 'unmourned and unmarked'. The poet then comments that Agamemnon persuaded Menelaus aisima pareipōn, 'advising what was due'. Leaf notes how rare such moral judgements by the narrator are and sets beside it 23.176, where Akhilleus' killing of twelve Trojan youths is called 'evil deeds'; for him aisima means only what is due in retribution, not an absolute moral standard. Readers differ on how far this is moral approval: the poet may simply record the normal heroic view that the Trojans, who have condoned Paris' crime, must bear the consequences of defeat, and some hear irony. Agamemnon then spears the suppliant himself.

anchor: upon the knees of fair-haired Athene
title: The robe (peplos) for Athena and twelve heifers
greek: πέπλον... θεῖναι Ἀθηναίης ἐπὶ γούνασιν (peplon... theinai Athēnaiēs epi gounasin); ἤνις ἠκέστας (ēnis ēkestas)
short: Helenus tells Hector to have Hecabe lay the finest robe on the knees of Athena's statue and vow twelve heifers; it is the only cult statue in Homer.
body: Laying a robe 'upon the knees' implies a seated image of the goddess. Leaf calls this the only allusion to a cult-statue in Homer and notes that Strabo (13.1.41, p. 601) defended the reading by listing ancient seated statues of Athena at Phocaea, Massalia, Rome, Chios and elsewhere; Monro also takes the statue as seated. Dressing images with costly robes is a widespread practice; Leaf mentions, but does not insist on, the parallel of the peplos woven for Athena at the Athenian Panathenaea. The vow promises twelve heifers ēnis ēkestas. Monro gives the traditional renderings 'yearlings' and 'untouched by the goad' (never yoked) but admits the true meaning is doubtful. The prayer will be refused (6.311).

title: Lycurgus and Dionysus
greek: Δρύαντος υἱὸς κρατερὸς Λυκόοργος (Druantos huios krateros Lukoorgos); Διώνυσος (Diōnusos)
short: Diomedes refuses to fight a god, recalling Lycurgus, who chased the nurses of 'mad' Dionysus and was blinded by Zeus.
body: Lycurgus, son of Dryas (in later tradition a Thracian king of the Edonians, as in Sophocles, Antigone 955-65), drove the nurses of Dionysus over 'sacred Nysa', beating them with an ox-goad; the god fled into the sea and was received by Thetis. Leaf notes that Dionysus is almost a stranger to the Homeric pantheon and reads the story as one of several myths about resistance to his orgiastic cult (compare Pentheus at Thebes); he considered 6.130-40 a late addition. The 'nurses' anticipate the later maenads, and Nysa was a mystic mountain placed wherever the cult travelled. Diomedes says nothing of his own fights with gods in Book V and chooses an unfamiliar exemplum instead. The contradiction with Book V, where he wounded Aphrodite and Ares, was noticed in antiquity; Leaf calls it one of the most patent in the Iliad.

title: 'As are the generations of leaves, so are those of men'
greek: οἵη περ φύλλων γενεὴ τοίη δὲ καὶ ἀνδρῶν (hoiē per phullōn geneē toiē de kai andrōn)
short: Asked his lineage, Glaucus answers that human generations come and go like leaves, one of the most quoted lines in Greek poetry.
body: Diomedes asks who Glaucus is; Glaucus first questions the value of pedigree itself. The wind scatters one year's leaves, the forest puts out new ones in spring, and so one human generation grows while another dies. Leaf calls it one of the most imitated comparisons in Homer: an early elegist, probably Simonides, quotes the line as the finest saying of 'the man of Chios' (preserved by Stobaeus); Mimnermus (fr. 2) and Aristophanes (Birds 685-7) rework it; Apollo uses the same image at 21.464-6; Virgil turns it into the souls crowding the Styx (Aeneid 6.309-12), and Milton's fallen angels lie 'thick as autumnal leaves' (Paradise Lost 1.302-4). Van Nortwick and Steadman stress that a character, not the narrator, voices this detachment, which prepares for the peaceful outcome.

title: Anteia and Bellerophon: the 'Potiphar's wife' story
greek: Ἄντεια (Anteia); Προῖτος (Proitos)
short: Proetus' wife Anteia desires Bellerophon; refused, she accuses him of attempted rape, the folk-tale pattern of Joseph and Potiphar's wife.
body: Bellerophon, grandson of Sisyphus, is driven from Argos by King Proetus, whose wife Anteia (called Stheneboea in later tradition, Leaf notes) 'lusted madly' for him. When he refuses because his heart is 'upright' (agatha phroneonta), she tells her husband the opposite. Leaf identifies the widespread romance pattern, best known from Joseph and Potiphar's wife (Genesis 39) and Phaedra and Hippolytus. Proetus, reluctant to kill a guest-friend because 'his soul had awe of that', sends him to Lycia to be killed by others. The story of a wronged hero sent on deadly tasks is a familiar folk-tale structure, as Van Nortwick and Steadman observe of the three trials that follow. The embedded narrative also echoes the poem's main plot: a woman's desire and a broken bond of hospitality lie behind the Trojan War too.

title: 'Baneful signs' on a folded tablet: writing in Homer?
greek: σήματα λυγρά, γράψας ἐν πίνακι πτυκτῷ (sēmata lugra, grapsas en pinaki ptuktōi)
short: Proetus scratches 'many deadly signs' on a folded tablet for Bellerophon to carry: the only clear allusion to something like writing in Homer.
body: The phrase is much debated. Grapsas means 'scratching' or 'incising' (Seymour notes that graphō is used of cutting and scratching as well as writing), and sēmata are 'signs', so the message might be pictographic. Leaf, writing after Arthur Evans' discoveries of Aegean scripts in Crete, thought the passage must imply a knowledge of writing, though not its literary use, and suggested that writing may be imagined as a kind of magic. Monro called the evidence indecisive but noted the folding tablet (later the wax-covered diptych). Seymour and Monro also connect the sēmata with the guest-token (tessera hospitalis) that a stranger carried to his host, so that 'baneful tokens' becomes an oxymoron. The king asks to 'see the sign' only after nine days of hospitality (6.174-7). Van Nortwick and Steadman point out the relevance for theories of how the Iliad itself was composed.

title: The Chimaera
greek: Χίμαιρα ἀμαιμακέτη (Chimaira amaimaketē)
short: Bellerophon's first task: the fire-breathing Chimaera, lion in front, serpent behind, goat (chimaira) in the middle; the only mixed monster Homer describes.
body: The word chimaira means 'she-goat', and the monster is 'of divine stock': lion in front, snake behind, goat in the middle, breathing fire. Leaf notes that this is the only place where Homer formally describes one of the composite monsters so common in later Greek myth, and that the couplet 6.181-2 recurs word for word in Hesiod (Theogony 319-25, at 323-4), where the Chimaera is the child of Echidna and is killed by Bellerophon and Pegasus. Homer does not mention Pegasus, who is central in Pindar's version (Olympian 13.63-92). Monro reads amaimaketē as an intensive 'monstrous, huge'. A later passage says the Chimaera was reared by Amisodarus of Lycia (16.328-9). After the Chimaera Bellerophon defeats the Solymi and the Amazons, 'the peers of men', and survives an ambush, three trials in the familiar folk-tale pattern.

title: Bellerophon on the Aleian plain
greek: κὰπ πεδίον τὸ Ἀλήϊον οἶος ἀλᾶτο (kap pedion to Alēion oios alato)
short: Hated by the gods, Bellerophon wandered alone over the 'Plain of Wandering', 'devouring his own heart'; Milton recalls the line in Paradise Lost.
body: Homer does not say why Bellerophon 'came to be hated of all the gods'; later legend (Pindar, Isthmian 7.44-7) blames his attempt to ride Pegasus to heaven. Leaf and Monro note the pun: the Alēion plain is where he 'wandered' (alato, from alaomai). Herodotus (6.95) places an Aleian plain in Cilicia. The phrase 'devouring his own heart' (thumon katedōn) describes melancholy isolation; Leaf mentions Cicero's Latin version (Tusculan Disputations 3.63) as a classic description of grief. Milton prays not to share Bellerophon's fate: 'Lest from this flying steed unreined... Dismounted, on th' Aleian field I fall, / Erroneous there to wander and forlorn' (Paradise Lost 7.17-20). In Glaucus' story the fall is set beside the deaths of Bellerophon's children, a reminder that heroic success does not last.

title: 'Ever to be best and pre-eminent above all'
greek: αἰὲν ἀριστεύειν καὶ ὑπείροχον ἔμμεναι ἄλλων (aien aristeuein kai hupeirochon emmenai allōn)
short: Glaucus' father's charge, repeated as Peleus' instruction to Akhilleus (11.784), sums up the competitive heroic ethic: always be the best.
body: Hippolochus 'straitly charged' his son to excel always and not to shame the race of his fathers. Leaf calls it a famous line; it recurs at 11.784, where Nestor recalls Peleus giving Akhilleus the same command. The verb aristeuein is the root of aristeia: to excel is to win the prize of being aristos, best, a status that must be shown and recognised in public. The second half of the charge, 'not to bring shame upon the race', links individual excellence with family honour, so that a hero's lineage, the subject of Glaucus' whole speech, is both a claim and an obligation. Leaf notes that the descendants of Glaucus later had prestige among the Ionians, some of whom, according to Herodotus (1.147), chose kings from his line. Sarpedon's speech to Glaucus at 12.310-28 develops the same ethic.

title: Xenia: guest-friends from their fathers' time
greek: ξεῖνος πατρώϊος (xeinos patrōïos); ξενία (xenia)
short: Diomedes learns that his grandfather Oeneus once hosted Bellerophon: the two enemies are hereditary guest-friends and agree not to fight.
body: Xenia, guest-friendship, was a binding relationship between men of different communities, created by hospitality and gifts and passed down to descendants. Oeneus entertained Bellerophon for twenty days, and they exchanged gifts: a purple belt and a two-handled golden cup, which Diomedes still keeps at home. Diomedes was a child when Tydeus left for Thebes and does not remember him (6.222-3), which is why the bond runs through Oeneus, his grandfather. The bond overrides the war: each promises to avoid the other 'even amid the throng', since there are plenty of other men to kill. Leaf also notes the Homeric custom of entertaining a guest for days before asking his name (6.174-5; compare Odyssey 7.237-9, 8.550). The scene contrasts with Paris, whose abuse of Menelaus' hospitality caused the war.

title: Gold for bronze: the exchange of armour
greek: χρύσεα χαλκείων, ἑκατόμβοι᾽ ἐννεαβοίων (chrusea chalkeiōn, hekatomboi' enneaboiōn)
short: Zeus 'took away the wits' of Glaucus, who gave golden armour worth a hundred oxen for bronze worth nine; the phrase became proverbial.
body: Value is reckoned in oxen, the standard measure of wealth in Homer (Leaf). The narrator's comment that Zeus 'took away his wits' has puzzled readers. Leaf finds it an outbreak of deliberate humour; Monro remarks that the idea of romantic generosity is foreign to the Iliad, and any strange act is ascribed to a god. Plato quotes 'gold for bronze' as a proverb for a bad bargain (Symposium 219a), and Seymour adds Cicero (Letters to Atticus 6.1.22) and Horace (Satires 1.7.15-18). Modern readings vary: Walter Donlan studied the 'unequal exchange' in terms of the Homeric gift economy (Phoenix 43, 1989, 1-15). The episode closes Diomedes' aristeia.

title: Priam's palace
greek: πεντήκοντ᾽ ἔνεσαν θάλαμοι ξεστοῖο λίθοιο (pentēkont' enesan thalamoi xestoio lithoio)
short: Priam's house holds fifty chambers for his sons and their wives and twelve for his daughters and their husbands: an image of Troy's wealth and continuity.
body: The description is the most detailed of any Trojan building and comes just as Hector enters the city. Leaf explains that the sons' bedrooms are inside the house itself, while the twelve chambers for the sons-in-law are across the courtyard; he compares the extra rooms added to the palace at Tiryns and the 'joint family' household known from India, where sons stay under the father's roof while he lives. The number fifty matches Priam's fifty sons (24.495). Van Nortwick and Steadman read the passage as a picture of Troy's civilisation at its height, its wealth and fertility, just before we watch Hector take leave of it. The palace's later fate is known to every listener: Priam will be killed in his own house and his sons' wives taken as slaves, as Hector foresees for Andromache (6.454-8).

title: Wine, libation and unwashed hands
greek: χερσὶ δ᾽ ἀνίπτοισιν Διὶ λείβειν αἴθοπα οἶνον ἅζομαι (chersi d' aniptoisin Dii leibein aithopa oinon hazomai)
short: Hector refuses his mother's wine: it would weaken him, and he dare not pour a libation to Zeus with hands fouled by blood.
body: Hecabe offers 'honey-sweet wine' for a libation and for strength. Hector declines on two grounds. Practically, wine would 'cripple' him (apoguiōsēis, literally 'unlimb'); Leaf comments that Hector was 'on the level of the present day' in seeing the disadvantage of stimulants in severe fatigue. Religiously, he feels awe (hazomai) at pouring wine to Zeus with unwashed hands, 'befouled with blood and filth'. Hesiod's Works and Days (724-5) forbids libations to Zeus with unwashed hands, and Homeric heroes regularly wash before prayer (compare 16.228-30, 24.302-5). Van Nortwick and Steadman see a symbolic meaning too: the warrior's blood both marks his role and separates him from the city he defends. Hector's refusals here begin a sequence in which each person he meets in Troy tries to hold him back.

title: Sidonian robes and Herodotus' Homeric criticism
greek: πέπλοι παμποίκιλα ἔργα γυναικῶν Σιδονίων (peploi pampoikila erga gunaikōn Sidoniōn)
short: Hecabe's robes were made by women of Sidon, brought by Paris on his voyage home with Helen; Herodotus used these lines as evidence about Homer.
body: Phoenician Sidon was famous for fine craftsmanship (compare the Sidonian bowl at 23.743), and Monro notes that Homer names Sidon several times but never Tyre. The lines imply that Paris sailed home from Sparta by way of Phoenicia. Herodotus (2.116) quotes 6.289-92 'from the Aristeia of Diomedes', along with lines from Odyssey Book 4, to argue that Homer knew the Egyptian story that Helen spent the war in Egypt, and therefore that the epic Cypria, in which Paris reached Troy in three days, was not by Homer. Leaf treats this as the oldest piece of Homeric criticism we have. The robe Hecabe chooses 'shone like a star' and lay at the bottom of the chest, a sign of its value: the Trojans offer the most precious object they own.

title: Athena refuses the Trojan women's prayer
greek: ἀνένευε δὲ Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη (aneneue de Pallas Athēnē)
short: Theano, Antenor's wife and Athena's priestess, lays the robe on the statue and prays, but Athena 'nodded up', the Greek gesture for no.
body: Theano, daughter of Cisseus and wife of the Trojan elder Antenor (5.70, 11.224), holds a public priesthood; Leaf notes that her office looks as much civic as religious. The women raise the ritual cry (ololugē) and she asks Athena to break Diomedes' spear. The verb ananeuein means to throw the head back, the gesture of refusal still used in Greece today (Leaf, Monro). Some ancient critics took it to mean that the statue itself moved; Leaf thinks the word is simply the normal metaphor for refusing. Virgil remembers the scene in the Aeneid, where the Trojan women bring a robe to Pallas, who keeps her eyes fixed on the ground (1.479-82). The audience knows that Athena is the Achaeans' strongest ally; the refusal, stated in a single line, is one of the grimmest moments in the book.

title: 'Strange man' (daimonie)
greek: δαιμόνιε / δαιμονίη (daimonie / daimoniē)
short: Daimonie, literally 'touched by a daimon', is an address of reproach or concern; Hector, Andromache and Paris use it to one another in this book.
body: LSJ explains daimonios as 'of a daimōn' (a divine power), and in Homer used only in the vocative as an address to chiefs or commoners, sometimes between husbands and wives (6.407, 6.486; Priam to Hecabe at 24.194). The tone depends on context: it implies that the person is behaving strangely, as if possessed. Monro says it expresses painful surprise and that, applied to Paris, Hector's suggestion that his brother is sulking in 'anger' is ironical politeness that avoids calling him a coward. Leaf calls the word in Andromache's mouth 'really untranslatable'; Murray renders it 'Ah, my husband' (6.407) and 'Dear wife' (6.486). Van Nortwick and Steadman read the repeated address as a sign that husband and wife are 'strange' to each other, each unable to enter the other's world.

title: Helen's self-reproach: 'me, a dog'
greek: δᾶερ ἐμεῖο κυνὸς κακομηχάνου ὀκρυοέσσης (daer emeio kunos kakomēchanou okruoessēs)
short: Helen calls herself a 'dog', the strongest Homeric term of shameless behaviour, and wishes she had died at birth.
body: To call someone a dog in Homer is to accuse them of shamelessness; Akhilleus calls Agamemnon 'dog-faced' (1.159, 1.225), and Helen uses the same self-abuse at 3.180 and Odyssey 4.145. Leaf and Monro discuss the adjectives: kakomēchanos, 'contriver of evil', and okruoeis, which Monro explains as 'a thing of horror', from kruos 'chill'. Helen wishes a storm-wind had swept her away at birth (compare the Harpies carrying off Pandareus' daughters, Odyssey 20.61-82, Leaf). She contrasts Paris, who has no sense of nemesis, the indignation of others, with Hector, who bears most of the trouble. Helen is the most self-critical character in the poem: others blame the gods for her (3.164), but she blames herself and Paris. The speech ends with her famous awareness of becoming a theme of song (6.357-8).

title: 'A song for men that are yet to be'
greek: ἀνθρώποισι πελώμεθ᾽ ἀοίδιμοι ἐσσομένοισι (anthrōpoisi pelōmeth' aoidimoi essomenoisi)
short: Helen says Zeus gave her and Paris an evil fate so that they would be a subject of song for future generations: the poem reflecting on itself.
body: This is one of the clearest moments in which a Homeric character imagines her own afterlife in poetry. The adjective aoidimos, 'sung of', is used here in a bad sense, 'notorious' (LSJ, citing 6.358); later Greek uses it for 'famous in song'. Seymour and Leaf compare Alcinous' words in the Odyssey, that the gods spun destruction for men 'so that there might be song for those to come' (8.579-80), and the contrast in Odyssey 24.196-202 between the glorious song of Penelope and the hateful song of Clytemnestra. Helen thus links suffering, divine will and kleos: the price of being remembered is the disaster that makes the story. Readers of the Iliad are, in effect, the 'men yet to be' she addresses.

anchor: he burnt him in his armour
title: Eëtion's funeral: Akhilleus honours his victim
greek: οὐδέ μιν ἐξενάριξε, σεβάσσατο γὰρ τό γε θυμῷ (oude min exenarixe, sebassato gar to ge thumōi)
short: Andromache's father Eëtion, king of Thebe under Placus, was killed by Akhilleus, who out of awe burned him in his armour and raised a mound.
body: Thebe 'under wooded Placus' lay in the plain of Adramyttium south of Troy; Leaf notes the later name 'plain of Thebe' (Herodotus 7.42), and Monro and Leaf agree that these Cilicians have nothing to do with historical Cilicia. Akhilleus sacked the city (1.366-9, where Chryseis was taken), killed Eëtion and his seven sons, and ransomed his widow. Instead of stripping the body, the usual practice, he 'had awe' (sebassato) and burned it with the armour, raising a sēma (barrow); mountain nymphs planted elms around it. Leaf explains that burying arms with the dead is an old custom surviving into the practice of cremation, and that elms were regarded as funereal trees. The story shows an earlier, more restrained Akhilleus, a contrast with his treatment of Hector's corpse later (Van Nortwick and Steadman).

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 1 (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1900), notes on 6.397, 6.418 and 6.419

title: Scamandrius and Astyanax, 'lord of the city'
greek: Σκαμάνδριος (Skamandrios); Ἀστυάναξ (Astuanax), 'lord of the city'
short: Hector calls his son Scamandrius after Troy's river; the people call him Astyanax, 'lord of the city', because 'only Hector guarded Ilios'.
body: The boy has two names. Scamandrius honours the river Scamander; Astyanax (astu, 'city', + anax, 'lord') honours his father's role as Troy's defender. Plato discusses the names in the Cratylus (392b-393a): since Homer says the Trojan men called him Astyanax (22.506-7), Socrates argues that this must be the 'more correct' name. Leaf notes that anax here means protector more than king, like 'shepherd of the people', and compares names given in compliment to a father, such as Telemachus ('far-fighter') and Eurysaces. Andromache will foresee that he is thrown from the walls (24.734-5).

sources.cite: Plato, Cratylus 392b-393a

title: 'You are my father, mother, brother and husband'
greek: Ἕκτορ ἀτὰρ σύ μοί ἐσσι πατὴρ καὶ πότνια μήτηρ ἠδὲ κασίγνητος (Hektor atar su moi essi patēr kai potnia mētēr ēde kasignētos)
short: Having lost her whole family to Akhilleus, Andromache tells Hector that he is everything to her and begs him to stay on the wall.
body: Andromache's speech moves from her losses to a single conclusion: if Hector dies she will have no one. Its climax, 'you are to me father and queenly mother and brother, and my strong husband', was imitated many times. Leaf and Monro point to Sophocles' Ajax (514-19), where the captive Tecmessa says to Ajax that she has no homeland or family but him, and to echoes in Latin poetry (Ovid, Heroides 3.51; Propertius 1.11.23). Leaf adds that the whole of Tecmessa's speech is full of reminiscences of this scene. The appeal shows why the stakes are personal: Hector's death will turn Andromache into the widow and slave he imagines at 6.454-8. Her plea to 'have pity' (eleaire) prepares for his reply about shame and duty.

Sophocles, Ajax 514-19

title: The wild fig-tree: Andromache's tactical advice
greek: παρ᾽ ἐρινεόν (par' erineon)
short: Andromache urges Hector to station the army by the wild fig-tree where the wall is weakest; ancient critics thought a woman should not give such advice.
body: The erineos (wild fig) is a landmark on the plain near the Scaean gate (11.167, 22.145). Andromache says the best Achaeans have three times tried to scale the wall there. Aristarchus athetised (marked as spurious) 6.433-9, Leaf reports, on two grounds: that it is unfitting for Andromache to act as a rival commander to Hector, and that the wall is nowhere else said to be weak at this point. Leaf notes a modern objection, that the lines are an anticlimax after her emotional plea, but doubts it is decisive. Monro points out that this is the only reference in Homer to an assault on Troy's walls and suggests the passage inspired the story in Pindar (Olympian 8.31-46) that the section built by the mortal Aeacus would be the weak point. Van Nortwick and Steadman read the advice as Andromache's attempt to cross into Hector's world, which he will close off.

anchor: have I shame of the Trojans
title: Hector's aidos: shame before the Trojans
greek: αἰνῶς αἰδέομαι Τρῶας καὶ Τρῳάδας ἑλκεσιπέπλους (ainōs aideomai Trōas kai Trōiadas helkesipeplous)
short: Hector answers that his aidos before the Trojans and their 'long-robed' wives, and his own trained spirit, will not let him hang back like a coward.
body: Hector's reply defines the heroic motive in social terms: he feels aidōs, shame, before the men and the women of Troy (the women have 'trailing robes', helkesipeploi), and his own thumos 'does not suffer it', because he has 'learnt to be valiant always'. LSJ's gloss of aidōs, 'respect for the feeling or opinion of others', fits exactly. His aim is to win 'great glory' (kleos) for his father and himself. Leaf notes that Hector's only object here is honour, since he does not hope for final success. The same words return in his monologue before facing Akhilleus (22.105-7), where shame before the Trojans keeps him outside the walls. Van Nortwick and Steadman stress that he cannot stay with those he loves and still think of himself as a man; the scene is the clearest statement in the poem of how a shame culture binds even its best member.

title: 'The day shall come when sacred Ilios shall be laid low'
greek: ἔσσεται ἦμαρ ὅτ᾽ ἄν ποτ᾽ ὀλώλῃ Ἴλιος ἱρή (essetai ēmar hot' an pot' olōlēi Ilios hirē)
short: Hector knows Troy will fall, the same words Agamemnon used in confidence (4.164-5); Scipio was said to quote them as Carthage burned.
body: Hector speaks with certainty 'in heart and soul' that Troy, Priam and his people will perish. The two lines are spoken earlier by Agamemnon (4.164-5) as a prediction of Trojan punishment; in Hector's mouth the same words become tragic foreknowledge. He predicts the fall of Troy here and almost immediately afterwards prays for his son's future (6.476-81). Seymour records the famous later use: Scipio Aemilianus, watching Carthage burn in 146 BC, is said to have quoted these lines, thinking of Rome. The story goes back to the historian Polybius (38.22), who was with him, and is retold by Appian (Punica 132). Hector's greatest grief is not for Troy but for Andromache's future slavery (6.450-65).

sources.cite: Thomas D. Seymour, Homer's Iliad, Books IV-VI (Boston: Ginn, 1891), note on 4.164
Polybius 38.22; Appian, Punica 132

title: Messeis and Hypereia: Andromache as a slave in Greece
greek: ὕδωρ φορέοις Μεσσηΐδος ἢ Ὑπερείης (hudōr phoreois Messēïdos ē Hupereiēs)
short: Hector imagines Andromache weaving and fetching water at Greek springs as a captive, while someone points her out as 'the wife of Hector'.
body: Weaving at another woman's command and carrying water were the typical tasks of slave women. Messeis and Hypereia are springs in Greece whose location was disputed in antiquity: Leaf and Monro report that Pausanias saw a Messeis at Therapne in Laconia (3.20.1), and that Strabo says the people of Pharsalus showed both springs near their city. Leaf thinks Thessalian Argos is probably meant, while Monro notes that Hector's knowledge of Greek springs is a natural slip on the poet's part. Hector even imagines what a passer-by will say, 'This is the wife of Hector', so that his fame (kleos) becomes part of her suffering.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 1 (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1900), notes on 6.455-7

title: Astyanax frightened by the helmet
greek: ταρβήσας χαλκόν τε ἰδὲ λόφον ἱππιοχαίτην (tarbēsas chalkon te ide lophon hippiochaitēn)
short: The baby shrinks from his father's nodding horse-hair crest; both parents laugh, and Hector lays the helmet on the ground.
body: This is one of the few moments of laughter between mortals in the Iliad. The child does not recognise his father behind the bronze and the 'dreadfully nodding' crest. Monro analyses the sequence of participles: the child cries out, shrinks back because he is terrified, and is terrified because he notices the crest. Hector takes off the helmet and lays it 'all-gleaming' on the ground before kissing his son and praying. Van Nortwick and Steadman read the helmet as the symbol of war that Hector has brought into the city: he can embrace his son only by putting it aside, and he takes it up again when he sends Andromache home (6.494-5). The same helmet image returns when Patroclus' helmet, really Akhilleus', rolls in the dust (16.793-800).

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer: Iliad, Books I-XII (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1894 ed.), notes on 6.468-70
Thomas Van Nortwick and Geoffrey Steadman, Homer: Iliad 6 and 22 (Dickinson College Commentaries, 2018), essay on 6.466-502

title: Hector's prayer for his son
greek: πατρός γ᾽ ὅδε πολλὸν ἀμείνων (patros g' hode pollon ameinōn)
short: Hector prays that his son will rule Troy and that men will say 'he is far better than his father'; the audience knows the prayer will fail.
body: The prayer is a father's wish, but its content is entirely heroic: strength, kingship over Troy, blood-stained spoils, and a mother's pride. Leaf and Monro both prefer the optative eipoi ('may someone say') at 6.479 over the manuscripts' subjunctive, so that the line belongs to the prayer rather than a confident prediction. The prayer was imitated by Sophocles, whose Ajax prays that his son will be 'more fortunate than his father, but in all else like him' (Ajax 550-1, cited by Seymour), and by Virgil's Aeneas: 'learn courage from me, my son, and true labour; fortune from others' (Aeneid 12.435-6). There is a tension between Hector's certainty that Troy will fall (6.447-9) and these hopes. The listener knows that Astyanax will be killed when Troy falls (24.734-5).

title: 'Smiling through her tears'
greek: δακρυόεν γελάσασα (dakruoen gelasasa)
short: Two words in Greek, 'tearfully laughing', capture Andromache's mixed emotion as she takes back her child.
body: The phrase joins an adverb from dakruoeis, 'tearful', with gelasasa, 'having laughed' or 'breaking into a smile'. Leaf calls it 'a deservedly famous phrase', though he thought its emotional subtlety unlike the oldest epic style. The smile answers the laughter over the frightened child (6.471), the tears her earlier weeping (6.405). Seymour notes that the next phrase, 'her husband was touched with pity', uses an inceptive aorist: pity 'came over' Hector. The scene is the emotional centre of the book and has been imitated and quoted by poets ever since.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 1 (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1900), note on 6.484

title: Moira: no one escapes his fate
greek: οὐ γάρ τίς μ᾽ ὑπὲρ αἶσαν ἀνὴρ Ἄϊδι προϊάψει· μοῖραν δ᾽ οὔ τινά φημι πεφυγμένον ἔμμεναι ἀνδρῶν (ou gar tis m' huper aisan anēr Aïdi proïapsei; moiran d' ou tina phēmi pephugmenon emmenai andrōn)
short: Hector comforts Andromache: no one will kill him 'beyond his portion' (aisa), and no man, coward or brave, escapes his moira once born.
body: Moira and aisa both mean 'portion, share', and hence one's allotted fate, above all the time of death. Hector's comfort is double-edged: he will not die before his time, but his time will come, and courage or cowardice makes no difference. Monro explains ta prōta as 'once for all', from the moment of birth. Leaf cross-refers 'beyond his portion' (huper aisan) to 2.155, where the Greeks almost sail home 'beyond fate'; the Iliad several times imagines events happening against fate (16.780, 20.30, 20.336), only to have them prevented. The sentiment is a commonplace of Greek consolation, but here, from a man about to return to battle, it is bleak. Van Nortwick and Steadman note that Hector cannot step outside the heroic perspective even to comfort the person he loves. Compare Sarpedon's reflection on mortality at 12.322-8.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 1 (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1900), notes on 6.487-9
D. B. Monro, Homer: Iliad, Books I-XII (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1894 ed.), notes on 6.488-9
Thomas Van Nortwick and Geoffrey Steadman, Homer: Iliad 6 and 22 (Dickinson College Commentaries, 2018), essay on 6.466-502

title: 'War shall be the concern of men'
greek: πόλεμος δ᾽ ἄνδρεσσι μελήσει (polemos d' andressi melēsei)
short: Hector sends Andromache back to her loom and distaff: war is for men, and for him most of all; the lines are reused three times in the Odyssey.
body: Hector's dismissal divides the world into the household, where women weave and supervise servants, and the battlefield, where men fight. Leaf notes that the lines are adapted in the Odyssey, where Telemachus tells Penelope that speech (muthos, 1.356-9) and the bow (21.350-3) are the business of men, and Alcinous says the same of sending Odysseus home (11.352-3); Leaf thinks the Iliad passage is the original, since the context suits it best. Monro and Leaf cite the echo in Aeschylus, Seven against Thebes 200-1, and Monro notes Aristophanes' parody in Lysistrata 520. Andromache's tactical advice (6.433-9) had briefly crossed this line; Hector closes it, and then puts his helmet back on. The words are a statement of gender roles, but also of Hector's isolation.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 1 (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1900), notes on 6.490-3
D. B. Monro, Homer: Iliad, Books I-XII (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1894 ed.), note on 6.492

title: Lament for a living man
greek: αἳ μὲν ἔτι ζωὸν γόον Ἕκτορα ᾧ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ (hai men eti zōon goon Hektora hōi eni oikōi)
short: Andromache's servants raise the ritual lament (goos) for Hector in his own house while he is still alive, anticipating his funeral in Book XXIV.
body: The goos is the formal lament sung by women over the dead, led by the closest female relative; the full ceremony for Hector, with laments by Andromache, Hecabe and Helen, closes the poem (24.719-76). Here it is performed in advance, because the women believe he will never return. Leaf and Monro discuss the unusual verb form goon, probably an aorist meaning 'they wailed'. The line turns the domestic scene into a funeral and makes Hector, still alive, already a figure of memory. It also shows the women's knowledge of what war means, in contrast to the hopes in Hector's prayer. Andromache's walk home, 'oft turning back' (entropalizomenē, 6.496), adds a single gesture of reluctance to leave him.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 1 (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1900), note on 6.500
D. B. Monro, Homer: Iliad, Books I-XII (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1894 ed.), note on 6.500

title: Simile: Paris as a stallion breaking free
greek: ὡς δ᾽ ὅτε τις στατὸς ἵππος ἀκοστήσας ἐπὶ φάτνῃ (hōs d' hote tis statos hippos akostēsas epi phatnēi)
short: Paris, gleaming in his armour, runs to battle like a well-fed horse that breaks its halter and gallops proudly to the mares' pasture.
body: The stalled horse (statos), fed on barley (akostēsas, a rare dialect word), breaks its tether and gallops to its favourite river and to the pastures of the mares, 'glorying in its splendour'. Leaf notes that the same simile is used of Hector returning to battle at 15.263-8 but thinks it belongs here first. Applied to Paris, it catches his vanity and sexual energy as well as his speed; Van Nortwick and Steadman stress how the repeated lines take on different colour in each context. Virgil uses it for Turnus arming (Aeneid 11.492-7). Leaf discusses the old claim that the dactylic rhythm imitates a gallop and warns against pressing it too far, since a Greek would have heard the hexameter as stately rather than galloping. Paris then greets Hector with breezy apologies (6.518-19).

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 1 (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1900), notes on 6.505-11
D. B. Monro, Homer: Iliad, Books I-XII (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1894 ed.), notes on 6.506-11

title: The 'mixing-bowl of freedom'
greek: κρητῆρα στήσασθαι ἐλεύθερον (krētēra stēsasthai eleutheron)
short: Hector hopes they may one day set up a krater of freedom, a celebratory bowl of wine for the gods, once the Achaeans are driven from Troy.
body: A krater was the large bowl in which wine was mixed with water for a feast and for libations. Hector imagines a victory celebration at which wine is mixed in honour of the gods 'that are for ever', marking Troy's freedom. Leaf and Monro note that eleutheros occurs in Homer only in this phrase and in the 'day of freedom' (eleutheron ēmar, 6.455, 16.831, 20.193); Monro translates 'a bowl in honour of deliverance'. The phrase answers Hector's earlier vision of Andromache robbed of her 'day of freedom' and ends the book on a hope the audience knows to be vain. It also restores, briefly, the bond between the two brothers, although Hector's words to Paris remain sharp: he is valiant but 'of thine own will slack' (6.521-3).
